MA342 overview

MA342 Topic Guide

Topological Spaces

Make topology axioms and standard examples automatic.

Purpose

State the topology axioms exactly and distinguish standard, cofinite, discrete, indiscrete and lower-limit examples.Exam use: The 2025/26 paper gives 4 marks for the topology definition, then asks for named topologies and a justified comparison rather than an axiom check on a finite family.

Question plan

  1. Write the proposed family τ and the underlying set X.
  2. Check ∅, X, arbitrary unions and finite intersections.
  3. For a named topology, state which sets are open rather than relying on a picture.
  4. For a comparison, give one decisive set that is open in one topology but not the other.
  5. Question interpretation: “Define” requires the full family of open sets; “coincide?” requires a yes/no conclusion and a separating example.

Definitions

A topology τ on X contains ∅ and X, is closed under arbitrary unions and finite intersections. Its members are open; complements of open sets are closed. The standard topology on R consists of arbitrary unions of open intervals. The cofinite topology on X is {∅} together with all U⊆X for which X\U is finite. The discrete topology is P(X), while the indiscrete topology is {∅,X}. A basis for the lower-limit topology on R is {[a,b):a<b}.Rapid recall: Name the underlying set, define the whole open-set family, and use an explicit witness when comparing two topologies.

Proof method

For finite candidate families, list the nontrivial unions and intersections. To disprove a topology, one failed axiom is enough.Exam workflow: List candidate sets systematically for finite X, use the strongest closure test first, and name the exact family whose union/intersection fails.

Worked simple example

On X={a,b}, τ={∅,{a},X} is a topology: it contains ∅ and X; every union is in τ; the only nontrivial intersection is {a}∩X={a}.

Medium/hard paper-style synthesis

The standard and cofinite topologies on R do not coincide. The interval (0,1) is standard-open, but its complement (-∞,0]∪[1,∞) is infinite, so (0,1) is not cofinite-open. In fact every cofinite-open subset of R is standard-open because a finite subset of R is closed, but the preceding example shows the inclusion is strict.

Graduated exam bridges

1. Foundation: Is {∅,{a},{b},X} a topology on {a,b}? Check: it is discrete.

2. Exam style: On a finite X with at least two points, show the cofinite topology is discrete. Check: each singleton has finite complement, so is open.

Hard paper-style synthesis

Describe a basis for the lower-limit topology on R. The answer is the family of half-open intervals [a,b), a<b. Do not replace these by ordinary open intervals: that would generate the standard topology instead.

Practice question - definitions and comparison [10 marks]

Inspired by: MA342 2025/26 Q1(a-b). Task. (a) Define a topology on a set X. [4 marks] (b) Define the standard topology on R and the cofinite topology on an arbitrary X, then decide with justification whether they coincide on R. [6 marks]

Demand diagnosis and fastest route: use one mark-bearing clause for each topology axiom, define both named open-set families, then separate them with a standard-open set having infinite complement.

Worked answer: A topology τ on X is a family of subsets containing ∅ and X, closed under arbitrary unions and finite intersections. The standard topology on R consists of all unions of open intervals (equivalently, it is generated by the basis {(a,b):a<b}). The cofinite topology is {∅}∪{U⊆X:X\U is finite}. On R they do not coincide: (0,1) is standard-open, but R\(0,1) is infinite, so (0,1) is not cofinite-open.

Topic-specific trap: “finite intersections” and “arbitrary unions” are not interchangeable, and an unsupported “no” earns less than a concrete separating set.

Mistakes

  • Checking only unions of two sets and forgetting the arbitrary-union axiom.
  • Calling every subset open in the cofinite topology on an infinite set.
  • Confusing a basis with the full topology.
  • Recovery rule: A family can pass several sample unions and still fail an arbitrary-union axiom; on finite families, enumerate all distinct unions.

Checklist

  • I can state all topology axioms.
  • I can distinguish discrete, indiscrete and cofinite examples.
  • I can give one decisive counterexample to an axiom.
  • Final 60-second audit: Underlying set, all three axioms, any counterexample family and complement-based closed sets are explicit.

Past-paper note

High confidence: all three papers from 2023/24 through 2025/26 test the topology definition and named examples. In 2025/26, Q1(a-b) assigns 10 marks to topology, standard/cofinite definitions and their comparison, while Q2(a) assigns 3 marks to the lower-limit basis. Back to paper evidence.
